chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Aamir, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Bureyd ibn Zamra Al-Laysi, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the man who is occupied/busy from the midday prayer time: 'Should he hasten [the prayer] from the beginning of the day?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, when he knows that he will be occupied, so he should hasten it during the forenoon, all of it.'

key_terms.الزَّوَال: Midday; the time when the sun begins to decline from its zenith, marking the start of Dhuhr prayer time.
key_terms.صَدْرُ النَّهَارِ: The forenoon; the early part of the day, specifically the time before midday.
key_terms.يَشْتَغِلُ: To be occupied/busy; refers to being engaged in work or activities that prevent timely prayer.
key_terms.يُعَجِّلُ: To hasten/accelerate; to perform an act earlier than its standard or preferred time.

ai.seo_question: When is it permissible to pray Dhuhr early if one will be busy at midday?
ai.summary: Recorded in *Al-Kafi* by Shaykh al-Kulayni, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the principle of *taqdim* (preference) in prayer timing to avoid *ta'khir* (delay) due to necessity. It highlights the Shia juristic view that the forenoon period for Dhuhr is not merely a window but a distinct phase where early performance is meritorious when valid excuses for later prayer exist. This ruling underscores the practical flexibility within Shia fiqh to accommodate daily life while maintaining spiritual discipline.
